title: An orderly account (Luke 1:1–4)
hook: Luke writes to Theophilus, lover of God, so he may know the certainty

segments.voice: Yesterday, Judas Maccabeus prayed for his fallen soldiers, and we closed fifty days of kings, prophets and wisdom. Your line was a holy and wholesome thought. Whose names did you write down? Day four hundred forty-two, and a new block: the Gospel of Luke.

Most books of the Bible never tell you who wrote them, or why. They just begin. Luke is different. Before a single angel appears, before Bethlehem, there's a short preface, four verses that are one long, polished sentence in Greek, the kind that opened histories and medical treatises in that world. It's the writer stepping out from behind the curtain for a moment and telling you what he's doing. And he isn't writing to the world in general. He's writing to one person, by name.
screen: `MOST BOOKS JUST BEGIN.` → `FOUR VERSES, ONE GREEK SENTENCE.` → `WRITTEN TO ONE PERSON.`

segments.voice: Here's the opening in the Douay-Rheims: "Forasmuch as many have taken in hand to set forth in order a narration of the things that have been accomplished among us." Notice the first thing he says: others have already tried this. Many of them. He's not the first. Then he says where his material came from: from those who were eyewitnesses from the beginning, and ministers of the word. So Luke is not claiming to be an eyewitness himself. He's a careful second-generation writer who has, in his words, diligently traced everything from the start. And then: it seemed good to me also "to write to thee in order, most excellent Theophilus, That thou mayest know the verity of those words in which thou hast been instructed." Theophilus is a Greek name: theos, God, and philos, friend or lover. Friend of God. Was he a real person? Most excellent was a polite title for an official or a person of rank, so he may have been a real patron who paid for the copying. But since early centuries readers have also noticed that anyone who loves God fits the name, and Saint Ambrose said as much. Both can be true. And Theophilus already knows the story; he's been instructed. Luke writes so he can stand on solid ground. The Greek word for verity is asphaleia: firmness, safety, footing that won't slip. Luke wrote a second volume, too, the Acts of the Apostles, also addressed to Theophilus. The Gospel never names its author; early Christian writers name Luke, the companion called the most dear physician in the Letter to the Colossians. For the next fifty days, we'll read his account in order.
screen: `MANY HAVE TAKEN IN HAND.` · `FROM EYEWITNESSES, NOT AN EYEWITNESS.` · `THEOPHILUS: FRIEND OF GOD.` · `ASPHALEIA: SOLID FOOTING.` · then, large: `THAT THOU MAYEST KNOW THE VERITY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find one thing you're certain of. Settle, and breathe. Not everything. Not the whole Creed, unless that's where you are. Just one thing you could stand on if the floor shook. Maybe it's that someone loves you. That a certain kindness was real. That God was there in a particular moment. That truth matters. Let it come, and test it gently: does it hold? Then, after the bell, write it down, the way Luke wrote for Theophilus, so you'll have it on paper. If you pray, you can thank God for that solid ground. The bell holds the time.
Theophilus. Friend of God, the man Luke addressed his careful, orderly account to, drawing on eyewitnesses from the beginning. Today's word.
Your line: written for you. Today, read Luke's first four verses yourself, and put your own name where it says Theophilus. Day four hundred forty-two.

howItsDone: Catholics hear the Gospel of Luke read through at Sunday Mass every third year (Year C), and Luke's preface is proclaimed on a Sunday in Ordinary Time; his feast day is October 18.

myth: Luke says he was an eyewitness of everything he writes
he says he drew on eyewitnesses and ministers of the word, and traced it all carefully.
Luke addresses Acts to Theophilus too
Acts opens by addressing Theophilus again; the two books are a pair.
the Gospel names Luke as its author in its text
the text never names him; early Christian writers attribute it to Luke, Paul's companion.

fork.setup: you're Luke. many others have already written accounts of Jesus. what do you do?
options: trace everything carefully from the beginning and write an orderly account for Theophilus.
write a new story with no sources.
fork.reveal: it seemed good to me also, he says, having traced all things from the beginning, to write to thee in order.

original.note: Greek: Theophilus, friend of God or dear to God, from theos and philos.

trapdoor: what you thought: the boring bit before the Christmas story.
what it means: the writer tells you his method: others wrote first, he used eyewitnesses, and he wrote in order so a friend of God could stand on solid ground.
what a scholar hears: one long Greek period in the style of Hellenistic historians; asphaleia, certainty; the same Theophilus in Acts 1:1.

notes: Douay-Rheims wording of Luke 1:1 and 1:3–4 quoted from memory; please check.
Ambrose on Theophilus (that the Gospel is written for anyone who loves God): confirm the reference in his Expositio Evangelii secundum Lucam.
Authorship: early tradition (Irenaeus, the Muratorian fragment) names Luke; Colossians 4:14 'Luke the most dear physician' (Douay). Confirm.

Luke 1:1–4 read on the 3rd Sunday in Ordinary Time, Year C (with 4:14–21): confirm. Feast of St Luke, October 18 (its Gospel is Luke 10:1–9, not the preface; reviewer corrected howItsDone, which had said the preface is read on the feast).
'The kind that opened histories and medical treatises': scholars debate whether the preface is closer to historians' or to technical/scientific prefaces (Cadbury, Loveday Alexander). Confirm wording.
Pauline authorship of Colossians is debated; reviewer changed 'the companion Paul calls the most dear physician' to 'the companion called the most dear physician in the Letter to the Colossians'.
Block D (days 442–491) is fifty days; 'the next fifty days' stated.
